title: Choosing a needlepoint canvas count
subtitle: How the count affects finished size, thread choice, and working time
excerpt: Canvas count is the number of holes per 2.5 cm. It determines how large each stitch is, what finished size a design works out to, and how much thread the project uses. Three counts suit most needlepoint: 10, 13, and 18.
sourceNotes: Therese de Dillmont, Encyclopaedia of Needlework (1886), canvaswork chapter. Weldon's Practical Needlework, canvaswork series.

glossaryTerms.definition: The number of holes per 2.5 cm (1 inch) on needlepoint canvas. A higher count means finer holes, smaller stitches, and more detail possible.
Needlepoint canvas woven from single threads, with clear individual holes. It needs to be mounted on a frame and blocked after working.
Canvas woven with paired interlocked threads that resist distortion. More stable than mono canvas but slightly harder to pull thread through.

heroPrompt: Three samples of needlepoint canvas at different counts side by side, showing 10-count, 13-count, and 18-count with needles and wool samples beside them, natural light.

content.text: is the number of holes per 2.5 cm. A count of 10 has ten holes per 2.5 cm; a count of 18 has eighteen. Higher count means finer work, smaller stitches, and a finer finished texture. Lower count means larger, bolder stitches and faster coverage.

10-count canvas suits bold work, rug-weight designs, and beginners. Stitches are large and easy to see. One or two strands of tapestry wool sit well in each hole. A design on 10-count works out roughly 30% larger than the same design on 13-count.

13-count canvas is the standard weight for cushion fronts, chair pads, and most framed work. One strand of Persian wool, or two strands of tapestry wool, fills each hole. The finished texture is firm and detailed enough for most traditional needlepoint designs.

18-count canvas, sometimes called petit point canvas, suits very detailed fine work. One strand of stranded cotton or one fine wool strand fills each hole. Finished designs are much smaller than the chart, and the work takes considerably longer. Use a good magnifier and task lighting when working 18-count.
Mono canvas is a plain single-thread weave. It needs mounting on a scroll or slate frame because it distorts under the diagonal tension of tent stitch. It gives a clear, crisp stitch definition.

Interlock canvas pairs the threads and locks them at each intersection. It is more resistant to distortion and can be worked in a hoop rather than a frame for smaller pieces. The locked threads make the canvas slightly stiffer, which some people find harder to pull the needle through.

A correctly matched thread should slide into each hole without forcing but should sit snugly enough that the canvas threads between holes are covered. If the thread bunches or puckers the canvas, it is too thick. If canvas threads show between stitches after the work is complete, the thread is too thin.
As a guide: 10-count takes one or two strands of tapestry wool. 13-count takes one strand of Persian wool or two strands of tapestry wool. 18-count takes one strand of stranded cotton or a fine silk.

A design that is 100 stitches wide works out to 10 cm wide on 10-count canvas, 7.7 cm wide on 13-count canvas, and 5.6 cm wide on 18-count canvas. Divide the stitch count by the canvas count to get the finished size in inches, or multiply by 2.5 and divide by the count for centimetres.
